\chapter{Who Somebody Is}
\label{ch:ta-roles}
\hlchaptermodality{46}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what somebody's work is in Tamil, and recognise the endings that mark a man, a woman and respect.}

Complete TA-C46-guest and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[āsiriyar]{\ta{ஆசிரியர்} (āsiriyar) — a teacher}

\label{lesson:TA-C46-teacher}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{pal} mean, and what did \emph{vayiṟu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{ஆசிரியர்}}
\textbf{\ta{ஆசிரியர்}} (\emph{āsiriyar}) — \textquotedblleft{}a teacher\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{ācārya}, one who teaches by how they behave, arriving in Tamil with \emph{-ar} on the end — the respectful ending already met on \emph{ivar} and \emph{naṇbar}. So the word is polite before it is anything else: there is no way to say it that does not show regard.

Tamil keeps the older and plainer \ta{ஆசான்} (\emph{āsāṉ}) beside it, and that one is what a student of an art calls a master.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five ways to say who somebody is.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{āsiriyar}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{āsiriyar}, then \emph{naṇbar}, and hear the same ending on both
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{ஆசிரியர்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a teacher\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[māṇavaṉ]{\ta{மாணவன்} (māṇavaṉ) — a student}

\label{lesson:TA-C46-student}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{āsiriyar} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மாணவன்}}
\textbf{\ta{மாணவன்}} (\emph{māṇavaṉ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a student\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{māṇava}, 'a young person', with the \emph{-aṉ} Tamil puts on a male — the same \emph{-aṉ} as \emph{makaṉ} and \emph{naṇbaṉ}.

Change the ending and the person changes with it: \emph{māṇavi} is a girl studying, \emph{māṇavar} is said with respect or of more than one. One stem, three endings, and you already had all three.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: the one who teaches and the one who is taught.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{māṇavaṉ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{āsiriyar}, then \emph{māṇavaṉ}, so the pair sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{மாணவன்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a student\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[maruttuvar]{\ta{மருத்துவர்} (maruttuvar) — a doctor}

\label{lesson:TA-C46-doctor}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{māṇavaṉ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மருத்துவர்}}
\textbf{\ta{மருத்துவர்}} (\emph{maruttuvar}) — \textquotedblleft{}a doctor\textquotedblright{}.

This one is Tamil's own. It stands on \ta{மருந்து} (\emph{marundu}), 'medicine', and takes the same respectful \emph{-ar}: the person who deals in medicine.

Beside it sits \emph{vaittiyar}, from Sanskrit \emph{vaidya}, doing the same work with borrowed material. Where a language has both, it usually has a preference, and modern Tamil leans on \emph{maruttuvar} — the signboard on the hospital says so.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and the third one you hope to need rarely.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maruttuvar}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{māṇavaṉ}, then \emph{maruttuvar}, and hear the ending change
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{மருத்துவர்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a doctor\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vivasāyi]{\ta{விவசாயி} (vivasāyi) — a farmer}

\label{lesson:TA-C46-farmer}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{maruttuvar} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{விவசாயி}}
\textbf{\ta{விவசாயி}} (\emph{vivasāyi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a farmer\textquotedblright{}.

The ending is \emph{-i}, which Tamil hangs on somebody by their work rather than by their sex, so the one word covers a man and a woman alike.

The stem is borrowed. The inherited word is \ta{உழவன்} (\emph{uḻavaṉ}), built straight on \emph{uḻu}, 'to plough', and it carries an older weight — Tamil poetry praises the \emph{uḻavaṉ}, while a form at an office asks for the \emph{vivasāyi}. Two words, one occupation, two registers.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and the fourth one feeds the other three.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vivasāyi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{maruttuvar}, then \emph{vivasāyi}, and let the second end on \emph{-i}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{விவசாயி} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a farmer\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[viruntāḷi]{\ta{விருந்தாளி} (viruntāḷi) — a guest}

\label{lesson:TA-C46-guest}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{vivasāyi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{விருந்தாளி}}
\textbf{\ta{விருந்தாளி}} (\emph{viruntāḷi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a guest\textquotedblright{}.

Take it apart and the guest is named after the meal. The first half is \emph{virundu}, a feast laid on for somebody; the second is \emph{āḷi}, from \emph{āḷ}, 'a person'. A guest, in Tamil, is the person a feast is for — the obligation is inside the word, not added to it afterwards.

There is an older form too, \emph{viruntiṉar}, carrying the \emph{-ar} you now know well. Both say the same thing: somebody has arrived, and there will be food.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
That closes the run: a teacher, a student, a doctor, a farmer, a guest.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{viruntāḷi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{āsiriyar}, \emph{māṇavaṉ}, \emph{maruttuvar}, \emph{vivasāyi}, \emph{viruntāḷi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{விருந்தாளி} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a guest\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
